name: Demetrius and the silversmiths of Ephesus
charge: Raising an uproar over lost trade under the colour of zeal for Diana
summary: Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines for Diana, called the craftsmen of like occupation together and told them plainly that their wealth and their goddess were both at stake because Paul had persuaded much of Asia that gods made with hands are no gods (Acts 19:24-27). The city filled with confusion, Paul’s travelling companions were dragged into the theatre, and the crowd cried up Diana for about two hours (Acts 19:28-34). The townclerk quieted them, sent the craftsmen to the courts and the deputies, and dismissed the assembly; no sentence on Demetrius is recorded (Acts 19:35-41).
offenseFull: Demetrius made silver shrines for Diana and brought no small gain to the craftsmen, and when he gathered the workmen he said the quiet part first: by this craft we have our wealth (Acts 19:24-25). Only after that did he mention the goddess, whose temple was in danger of being despised because Paul was teaching throughout Asia that gods made with hands are no gods (Acts 19:26-27). Diana is the Roman name; the Greeks called her Artemis, and she is the same mother goddess our people have met under other names, the queen of heaven, Ishtar, Easter, the many breasted image of Asia Minor, worshipped in the same city where our people were set to pick cotton and tobacco. Her image was said to have fallen down from Jupiter (Acts 19:35), which is stone worship, the same practice the heathen still keep over a stone today. Paul was teaching the first commandments, that there is no other god and no image to bow to (Exodus 20:4), and the prophets had already priced the trade: they that make a graven image are all of them vanity, and their own witnesses see nothing (Isaiah 44:9-11). The parallel is not ancient. The pictures and statues sold as the Messiah bring no small gain today, and every year the stores panic when the presents are not moving. Take the idolatry out of the people’s minds and you have taken somebody’s money.

When they heard it they were full of wrath and cried that Diana was great, and the whole city was filled with confusion (Acts 19:28-29). Gaius and Aristarchus were caught and the crowd rushed into the theatre. Paul would have gone in to them and the disciples would not let him, and certain of the chief of Asia who were his friends sent word that he should not venture himself there (Acts 19:30-31): he kept friends with standing in these cities and they were worth something that day. The assembly itself was confused and the greater part did not know why they had come together (Acts 19:32), which is why the law says not to follow a multitude to do evil. When the Jews put Alexander forward to make a defence, the crowd would not hear a word once they knew what he was, and screamed for their goddess for about two hours (Acts 19:33-34). Two hours of a crowd shouting a name with no understanding in it is the same spirit that fills the so called Christian church.
judgmentFull: The townclerk appeased the people, but he did not correct them. He told them every man knew the city of the Ephesians was a worshipper of the great goddess Diana and of the image which fell down from Jupiter, and that these things could not be spoken against (Acts 19:35-36). He was of the same chief men of the city who had just sent Paul a warning as friends, and in the pinch he stood with the goddess. He then did the one useful thing: he said the men brought in were neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers, and that if Demetrius and his craftsmen had a matter against any man, the law was open and there were deputies, and other questions belonged in a lawful assembly (Acts 19:37-39).

He warned that the city itself could be called in question for that day’s uproar, since there was no cause they could give for it, and he dismissed the assembly (Acts 19:40-41). Nothing is recorded against Demetrius. What the record leaves standing is the trade and the goddess behind it. Ephesus was the seat of that worship, and it is the reason Paul afterwards charged that congregation that the women keep silence and learn in subjection, not usurping authority over the man (1 Corinthians 14:34; 1 Timothy 2:11-12): the sisters repenting there were coming out of a city built on woman worship, and they had to be converted out of it. Brothers who have walked the ruins report that the same little images are still sold on the spot.

taught.title: Isaiah 44: The Idol Maker's Folly and the Changed Name

text.text: And the same time there arose no small stir about that way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;
Whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth.
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.
And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
They that make a graven image are all of them vanity; and their delectable things shall not profit; and they are their own witnesses; they see not, nor know; that they may be ashamed.
Who hath formed a god, or molten a graven image that is profitable for nothing?
Behold, all his fellows shall be ashamed: and the workmen, they are of men: let them all be gathered together, let them stand up; yet they shall fear, and they shall be ashamed together.
And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.
And when Paul would have entered in unto the people, the disciples suffered him not.
And certain of the chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre.
Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.
And they drew Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. And Alexander beckoned with the hand, and would have made his defence unto the people.
But when they knew that he was a Jew, all with one voice about the space of two hours cried out, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.

And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
Seeing then that these things cannot be spoken against, ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly.
For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess.
Wherefore if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another.
But if ye enquire any thing concerning other matters, it shall be determined in a lawful assembly.
For we are in danger to be called in question for this day’s uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse.
And when he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection.
But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
